title: Applications of Trigonometry
learningObjective: Solve applications that require the use of trigonometry to find a side or angle.

faqs.question: Where do I start with a trigonometry word problem?
faqs.answer:
Start with a picture, not a formula. Sketch the situation and label what you know and what you want to find. Then look for the triangle hiding in the picture: is there a right angle (a wall, level ground, a horizontal line of sight), or do you just have three pieces of information about a triangle? Only then choose your tool — right-triangle trig from TE4, or the Law of Sines or Law of Cosines from TE5 — and finish by checking that your answer makes sense (faq-14).

Every application problem follows the same four moves — the picture always comes first.

faqs.question: What are the angle of elevation and the angle of depression?
faqs.answer:
Both angles are measured from a horizontal line, never from the vertical. The angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal and your line of sight to something above you. The angle of depression is the angle between the horizontal and your line of sight to something below you. Which one a problem uses depends only on who is doing the looking.

Both angles are measured from a horizontal line. The observer looks up at the plane (angle of elevation, teal); the pilot looks down at the observer (angle of depression, orange).

faqs.question: Why are the angle of elevation and the angle of depression equal?
faqs.answer:
Draw a horizontal line at each end of the line of sight. Those two horizontals are parallel, and the line of sight is a transversal crossing both, so the two angles form a Z — and alternate interior angles are equal. That means the angle of depression from the top always equals the angle of elevation from the bottom. This is useful because the angle you're handed is often outside your triangle, but it has an equal twin inside it.

The two horizontal lines are parallel and the line of sight cuts across both, tracing a Z. The two angles inside the Z are equal, so the angle of depression equals the angle of elevation.

faqs.question: How do I know whether a problem needs right-triangle trig or the Law of Sines/Cosines?
faqs.answer:
Ask two questions in order. First: is there a right angle in the picture? If so, use the right-triangle tools from TE4. If not, ask whether you already hold a complete opposite pair — a given angle and the given side directly across from it. If yes, use the Law of Sines; if no (you have SAS or SSS information), use the Law of Cosines.

Two questions decide the method: first, is there a right angle? If not, do you already hold an angle and the side directly across from it?

faqs.question: What does it mean for a real situation (tides, a Ferris wheel) to be modeled by a sine or cosine function?
faqs.answer:
Anything that repeats on a regular cycle — tides, a Ferris wheel, daily temperature — can be described by a sine or cosine function. Three numbers describe the cycle: the midline (the middle value — a vertical shift from FN4), the amplitude (how far it swings above and below the midline, from PF1), and the period (how long one full cycle takes, also from PF1). Written as a model: \( y = A\sin(Bt) + D \) (or a cosine), where \( |A| \) is the amplitude, \( D \) is the midline, and the period is \( \dfrac{2\pi}{B} \).

The three numbers that describe any repeating cycle: the midline (the middle value), the amplitude (how far it swings above and below), and the period (how long one full cycle takes).

faqs.question: What do I do when the angle I need isn't inside the triangle (like a pilot's angle of descent)?
faqs.answer:
Look for a horizontal line through the observer. It's parallel to the ground, so the line of sight acts as a transversal, and the angle of descent equals the angle at the other end of the line of sight — which sits inside your right triangle (alternate interior angles, faq-3). Then use the sides you know with an inverse trig function.

The angle the pilot needs (θ, measured down from her horizontal) sits outside the triangle. Because the horizontal is parallel to the ground, the same θ appears inside the triangle at the runway.

Worked Example — right triangle

A plane at 40,000 ft is a horizontal distance of 750,000 ft from the runway. Height (opposite) \( = 40{,}000 \); horizontal distance (adjacent) \( = 750{,}000 \).

\( \tan\theta = \dfrac{40{,}000}{750{,}000} \)

\( \theta = \arctan\!\left(\dfrac{40{,}000}{750{,}000}\right) \approx 3.05° \)

faqs.question: How do I find a height from an angle of elevation and a horizontal distance (and remember the observer's height)?
faqs.answer:
The height you want is opposite the angle of elevation, and the horizontal distance is adjacent to it — that's the tangent ratio: \( \tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{distance}} \), so height \( = \) distance \( \times \tan\theta \). That gives the height above the observer's eye level, so add the height of the observer's eyes at the end. (Make sure your calculator is in degree mode.)

The tangent of the 70° angle of elevation gives the height above the observer's eyes (teal); the observer's eye height is then added on. (The eye height is exaggerated here so you can see it.)

Worked Example — right triangle

An observer 1.5 m tall stands 67 m from the Seattle Space Needle. The angle of elevation to the top is \( 70° \).

Height above eye level: \( 67\tan 70° \approx 184.1 \) m

Add the observer's height: \( 184.1 + 1.5 \approx 185.6 \) m — about 186 m to the nearest meter.

faqs.question: How do I find a horizontal distance from an angle of depression?
faqs.answer:
By faq-3, the angle of depression from the cliff equals the angle of elevation from the ship, so it appears inside the right triangle at the ship. The cliff height is opposite that angle and the distance you want is adjacent — tangent again, but this time the unknown is in the denominator, so you divide: \( x = \dfrac{380}{\tan 9°} \). A small angle means a long distance, so a result of about 2.4 km fits a 9° angle.

True to scale: a 380 m cliff and a 9° angle of depression put the ship far from shore (about 2,399 m). The same 9° appears as the angle of elevation from the ship back up to the cliff top.

Worked Example — right triangle

Standing on a cliff 380 m above the sea, Sean sees a ship at an angle of depression of \( 9° \).

\( \tan 9° = \dfrac{380}{x} \)

\( x = \dfrac{380}{\tan 9°} \approx 2{,}399 \) m

faqs.question: How do I find an unknown angle when I know two sides (like the ladder and the wall)?
faqs.answer:
Use an inverse trig function (PF3, TE4). Decide which ratio fits the two sides you know, relative to the angle you want, then take the inverse. Here the wall (13 ft) is opposite the angle at the ground and the ladder (14 ft) is the hypotenuse, so sine is the match.

Drawn to scale: a 14 ft ladder just reaches the top of a 13 ft wall. The wall is opposite the angle at the ground and the ladder is the hypotenuse — a job for sine.

Worked Example — right triangle

A 14-foot ladder reaches the top of a 13-foot wall.

\( \sin\theta = \dfrac{13}{14} \)

\( \theta = \arcsin\!\left(\dfrac{13}{14}\right) \approx 68° \)

faqs.question: How do I solve an application with a non-right triangle when I know two angles and a side (the two airplanes)?
faqs.answer:
There's no right angle, and you know an angle and the side across from it, so use the Law of Sines (TE5). Match each side with the angle directly across from it: the side from airplane A to the airport (20 mi) is across from the \( 50° \) angle, and the side we want (airplane B to the airport) is across from the \( 45° \) angle.

Two angles and the side between airplane A and the airport are known (true to scale). No right angle here — the unknown side (orange) is across from the 45° angle.

Worked Example — Law of Sines

Airplane A is 20 miles from the airport. The angle at A is \( 45° \) and the angle at B is \( 50° \). Let \( d \) be B's distance to the airport.

\( \dfrac{d}{\sin 45°} = \dfrac{20}{\sin 50°} \)

\( d = \dfrac{20\sin 45°}{\sin 50°} \approx 18.5 \) miles

faqs.question: How do I solve one when I know all three sides (the campers), and why does rounding early cause trouble?
faqs.answer:
Three sides and no angles means the Law of Cosines first, to find one angle. After that you hold a complete opposite pair, so the Law of Sines can find a second angle, and subtracting from \( 180° \) gives the third. Keep extra decimal places through every step: rounding in the middle can shift the final answer.

The campers' tents form a triangle with all three sides known (true to scale) and no right angle — each angle is at a different camper.

Worked Example — Law of Cosines, then Law of Sines

Carlos (across from the 175 ft side): \( \cos C = \dfrac{153^2+201^2-175^2}{2(153)(201)} = \dfrac{33{,}185}{61{,}506} \approx 0.5395 \), so \( C \approx 57.35° \).

Travis (across from the 153 ft side): \( \dfrac{\sin T}{153} = \dfrac{\sin 57.35°}{175} \) gives \( \sin T \approx 0.7362 \), so \( T \approx 47.40° \). (The other candidate, \( 132.6° \), is impossible — it would push the angle sum past \( 180° \).)

Jean: \( 180° - 57.35° - 47.40° \approx 75.25° \).

Rounding trap: if you round the first two angles to \( 57° \) and \( 47° \) before subtracting, Jean comes out as \( 76° \) — but the accurate value is \( 75.25° \), about \( 75° \).

faqs.question: How do I find the maximum, minimum, and period from a trig model like the tide equation?
faqs.answer:
Read the model like a recipe. For \( d(t) = 2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) \): the constant \( 2 \) is the midline, the coefficient \( \tfrac{1}{2} \) in front of the sine is the amplitude, and the number multiplying \( t \) (here \( \tfrac{\pi}{6} \)) sets the period. Careful with notation: the sine applies to the whole product \( \tfrac{\pi}{6}t \), not just to \( \tfrac{\pi}{6} \).

The tide model d(t) = 2 + ½ sin(πt/6): the depth swings between 1.5 m and 2.5 m around a midline of 2 m, and one full tide cycle takes 12 hours.

Worked Example — reading a model

Maximum \( = \) midline \( + \) amplitude \( = 2 + \dfrac{1}{2} = 2.5 \) m (high tide)

Minimum \( = \) midline \( - \) amplitude \( = 2 - \dfrac{1}{2} = 1.5 \) m (low tide)

Period \( = \dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/6} = 12 \) hours, so there are \( \dfrac{24}{12} = 2 \) tide cycles in a day.

faqs.question: How do I build a sine or cosine model for something like a Ferris wheel?
How do I check that my answer is reasonable?
faqs.answer:
A few quick checks catch most mistakes. (1) In a right triangle the hypotenuse must be the longest side. (2) In any triangle the longest side is across from the largest angle and the shortest side is across from the smallest. (3) A triangle's angles add to \( 180° \) (a right triangle's two acute angles add to \( 90° \)). (4) Ask whether the size fits the story — a shallow \( 9° \) angle of depression should give a distance much larger than the cliff's height. (5) Make sure your calculator is in degree mode for degree problems. (6) Answer in a sentence with units.

A quick sanity check: the longest side is always across from the largest angle (orange), and the shortest side is across from the smallest angle (teal).

faqs.question: How does this section pull together TE4 and TE5?
faqs.answer:
TE6 introduces no new triangle formulas. Every problem here is one you already have the tools for — the new skill is recognizing which tool fits, and drawing the diagram that reveals it. The pilot, Space Needle, cliff, and ladder problems hide right triangles (TE4); the two airplanes and the campers are non-right triangles that need TE5's laws. The campers problem even uses both laws in a single solution.

TE6 introduces no new triangle math — it's about recognizing which of your tools fits the situation.

faqs.question: How does the periodic-modeling part connect to PF1 and FN4?
faqs.answer: The amplitude and period in the tide and Ferris wheel models are exactly PF1's amplitude and period, with period \( = \dfrac{2\pi}{B} \). The midline is FN4's vertical shift (the \( +2 \) or \( +61 \) added to the wave), and the Ferris wheel's upside-down cosine is FN4's vertical reflection (the negative sign in \( -60\cos \)). Nothing here is new — it's the same transformations, tied to a real situation.

faqs.question: Why do these applications matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: Surveyors, pilots, navigators, architects, and engineers use exactly these tools to find heights, distances, and angles they can't measure directly: a building's height from the ground, the glide angle for a landing, the distance to a ship, or a position fixed from two bearings. The periodic models show up in tides, sound and light waves, seasonal temperatures, alternating current, and amusement-ride design.

guided.title: Practice Drawing the Diagram First
guided.prompt: I'm learning to solve trigonometry word problems. Give me a short word problem about a ladder, ramp, or shadow — but don't solve it. Ask me to describe the diagram I would draw, label what is known and unknown, and tell you which triangle and which tool I would use. Then let me solve it and check my work. Give me a few more problems of increasing difficulty.

guided.title: Practice Angles of Elevation and Depression
guided.prompt: I'm learning about angles of elevation and depression. Give me a problem where I'm given an angle of depression, which is outside the triangle, and ask me how to find the equal angle inside the triangle. Ask me to explain WHY the two angles are equal before I calculate anything. Then check my setup and my answer, and give me two more problems.

guided.title: Choose the Right Method
guided.prompt: I sometimes can't tell which tool a word problem needs. Give me several triangle application scenarios — some with a right angle, some without. For each one, ask me whether I would use right-triangle trig, the Law of Sines, or the Law of Cosines, and why, BEFORE I compute anything. Check my reasoning and help me with any I get wrong.

guided.title: Practice a Multi-Step Non-Right Triangle Problem
guided.prompt: I'm learning to solve a triangle when I know all three sides, like three people in tents a known distance apart. Walk me through using the Law of Cosines for the first angle, the Law of Sines for the second, and subtraction for the third. Then show me what goes wrong if I round the first two angles too early, and give me a similar problem to try.

guided.title: Practice Modeling a Periodic Situation
guided.prompt: I'm learning to model real cycles with sine or cosine. Give me a situation like a tide, a Ferris wheel, or daily temperature. Ask me to find the midline, amplitude, and period from the description, decide whether sine or cosine fits, and write the model. Then have me check it by plugging in t = 0 and t = half a period.

stages.desc: Three quick reviews TE6 leans on: SOH-CAH-TOA (TE4), choosing a law (TE5), and reading a sinusoid (PF1). Skip any you already have.

stops.title: SOH-CAH-TOA and inverse trig
stops.target: In a right triangle, pick the ratio that links what you know to what you want: \(\sin = \tfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}\), \(\cos = \tfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}\), \(\tan = \tfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}\). Use \(\sin^{-1}\), \(\cos^{-1}\), \(\tan^{-1}\) to find an angle.
stops.cold: (1) Find the side opposite the \(35^\circ\) angle.[[graph:G1q]](2) Find \(\theta\) to the nearest tenth of a degree.[[graph:G1q2]]
stops.coldPlain: (1) A right triangle has a 35 degree angle and hypotenuse 15. Find the side opposite the 35 degree angle. (2) A right triangle has legs 6 (opposite theta) and 10 (adjacent to theta). Find theta.
stops.graphNote: Both problems have labeled right-triangle pictures. I'll describe them if you need more.
stops.solution: (1) Opposite and hypotenuse use sine: opp = 15 sin 35, about 8.6. (2) Opposite and adjacent use tangent: theta = tan^(-1)(6/10), about 31.0 degrees.
stops.mistake: Typing tan(6/10) instead of tan^(-1)(6/10) when looking for an angle.
stops.again: (1) Hypotenuse 20, angle \(50^\circ\): find the adjacent side. (2) Opposite 9, hypotenuse 14: find the angle.
stops.reflect: How do you decide between sin, cos, and tan before you touch the calculator?

stops.title: Which tool fits the triangle?
stops.target: Decide between right-triangle trig, the Law of Sines, and the Law of Cosines from what the picture shows (TE4 and TE5).
stops.cold: Which tool? (1) A right triangle with one leg 8 and the hypotenuse 13; find an angle. (2) A triangle with angles \(40^\circ\) and \(75^\circ\) and the side between them 12. (3) A triangle with sides 7 and 9 and the angle between them \(110^\circ\); find the third side.
stops.coldPlain: Which tool? (1) Right triangle, one leg 8 and hypotenuse 13, find an angle. (2) Triangle with angles 40 and 75 degrees and the side between them 12. (3) Triangle with sides 7 and 9 and the angle between them 110 degrees; find the third side.
stops.coldA: (1) Right angle: SOH-CAH-TOA (inverse sine or cosine). (2) No right angle, two angles and a side: Law of Sines (find the third angle first). (3) No right angle, SAS: Law of Cosines.
stops.solution: (1) There is a right angle, so use right-triangle trig. (2) No right angle; once you find the third angle (65 degrees), every side has a matched angle, so the Law of Sines. (3) SAS with no matched pair: Law of Cosines.
stops.mistake: Using SOH-CAH-TOA on a triangle that has no right angle.
stops.again: (1) Three sides 5, 6, 8; find the largest angle. (2) A ramp makes a right angle with the ground; you know the ramp length and the angle; find the height.
stops.againA: (1) SSS: Law of Cosines. (2) Right angle: SOH-CAH-TOA (sine).
stops.reflect: What is the first thing you look for in a picture to choose a tool?

stops.title: Read a sinusoid: midline, amplitude, period
stops.target: For \(y = A\sin(Bt) + D\) or \(y = A\cos(Bt) + D\): midline \(D\), amplitude \(|A|\), max \(D + |A|\), min \(D - |A|\), period \(\tfrac{2\pi}{B}\) (PF1).
stops.cold: The temperature \(t\) hours after 6 a.m. is \(T(t) = 65 + 12\sin\left(\tfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)\) degrees F. Find the midline, amplitude, maximum, minimum, and period.
stops.coldPlain: T(t) = 65 + 12 sin(pi t / 12). Find the midline, amplitude, maximum, minimum, and period.
stops.solution: Midline 65, amplitude 12, so the max is 77 and the min is 53. Period = 2 pi / (pi/12) = 24 hours.
stops.mistake: Reading the period as pi/12 instead of computing 2 pi divided by pi/12.
stops.reflect: Why does a negative sign in front of cos not change the amplitude?

stages.desc: Right-triangle situations first, then non-right ones, then periodic models.

stops.title: Draw it first: the ladder
stops.target: Turn a word problem into a labeled right triangle, then choose the ratio.
stops.cold: A \(24\) ft ladder leans against a wall and reaches \(21\) ft up the wall. What angle does the ladder make with the ground? (Round to the nearest tenth.)[[graph:T1q]]
stops.coldPlain: A 24 ft ladder leans against a wall and reaches 21 ft up the wall. What angle does the ladder make with the ground?
stops.note: Show your labeled sketch: which side is opposite, adjacent, or the hypotenuse (or which law applies), and say why. Check that the answer makes sense in the situation.
stops.graphNote: There's a labeled sketch on the page. I'll describe what I drew.
stops.solution: The ladder is the hypotenuse (24), the height on the wall is opposite the ground angle (21). sin theta = 21/24, theta = sin^(-1)(21/24), about 61.0 degrees.
stops.mistake: Using tangent with 24 as the adjacent side: the ladder is the slanted side, so it is the hypotenuse.
stops.again: A \(36\) ft ladder reaches \(33\) ft up a wall. Find the angle with the ground.
stops.stretch: For the 24 ft ladder, how far is its foot from the wall?
stops.reflect: What is one sign in the wording that a side is the hypotenuse?

stops.title: Angles of elevation and depression
stops.target: Both angles are measured from a horizontal line. Because the horizontal line through the observer is parallel to the ground, the angle of depression equals the angle of elevation at the other end.
stops.cold: Rosa stands on a cliff \(300\) m above a lake and sees a boat at an angle of depression of \(22^\circ\). How far is the boat from Rosa (along her line of sight)? Round to the nearest meter.[[graph:T2q]]
stops.coldPlain: Rosa stands on a cliff 300 m above a lake and sees a boat at an angle of depression of 22 degrees. How far is the boat from Rosa (line of sight)?
stops.note: Show your labeled sketch: which side is opposite, adjacent, or the hypotenuse (or which law applies), and say why. Check that the answer makes sense in the situation.
stops.graphNote: There's a labeled sketch on the page. I'll describe what I drew.
stops.solution: The 22 degree depression angle equals the angle of elevation at the boat. From the boat, 300 is opposite and the line of sight is the hypotenuse: sin 22 = 300/d, d = 300/sin 22, about 801 m.
stops.mistake: Putting the 22 degree angle at the top of the cliff inside the triangle (between the cliff and the line of sight); that angle is actually 68 degrees.
stops.again: Mateo is on the ground and sees a person on top of a \(1200\) ft cliff at an angle of elevation of \(25^\circ\). How far away is the person (line of sight)?
stops.stretch: How far is the boat from the base of the cliff (horizontal distance)?
stops.stretchA: \(\tan 22^\circ = \tfrac{300}{x}\), so \(x\approx 743\) m. The "how far" in the question decides which side you want.
stops.reflect: In your own words, why are the angle of depression and the angle of elevation equal?

stops.title: Angle of climb (an angle at the ground)
stops.target: Place the given angle where it is measured, label opposite and adjacent, and convert units at the end.
stops.cold: A plane takes off and climbs at \(15^\circ\). How far along the ground does it travel to reach \(10{,}000\) ft of altitude? Give feet and miles (\(1\) mi \(= 5280\) ft).[[graph:T3q]]
stops.coldPlain: A plane climbs at 15 degrees. How far along the ground does it travel to reach 10,000 ft? Give feet and miles (1 mile = 5280 ft).
stops.note: Show your labeled sketch: which side is opposite, adjacent, or the hypotenuse (or which law applies), and say why. Check that the answer makes sense in the situation.
stops.graphNote: There's a labeled sketch on the page. I'll describe what I drew.
stops.solution: Altitude is opposite the 15 degree angle and the ground distance is adjacent: tan 15 = 10000/x, x = 10000/tan 15, about 37,321 ft, which is about 7.1 miles.
stops.mistake: Multiplying 10000 by tan 15 instead of dividing.
stops.again: Climb angle \(18^\circ\), altitude \(15{,}000\) ft. Ground distance in feet and miles?
stops.reflect: A pilot descending measures the angle down from her horizontal. Where does that angle show up inside the triangle?

stops.title: Two observers: Law of Sines
stops.target: When two observers sight the same object, the baseline and two angles make an ASA triangle. Use the angle sum, then the Law of Sines.
stops.cold: Two fire towers are \(20\) miles apart. Ranger Chang sees the fire \(48^\circ\) from the line to the other tower; Ranger Lee sees it \(62^\circ\) from the line to Chang's tower. Which ranger is closer, and how far away is that ranger from the fire?[[graph:T4q]]
stops.coldPlain: Two fire towers are 20 miles apart. Ranger Chang sees the fire 48 degrees from the line to the other tower; Ranger Lee sees it 62 degrees from the line to Chang's tower. Which ranger is closer, and how far?
stops.note: Show your labeled sketch: which side is opposite, adjacent, or the hypotenuse (or which law applies), and say why. Check that the answer makes sense in the situation.
stops.graphNote: There's a labeled sketch on the page. I'll describe what I drew.
stops.coldA: Lee is closer, about \(15.8\) mi (Chang is about \(18.8\) mi).[[graph:S4]][[graph:T4s]]
stops.solution: Fire angle = 180 - 48 - 62 = 70, across from the 20 mi side. Chang's distance is across from Lee's 62 degree angle: 20 sin 62 / sin 70, about 18.8. Lee's distance is across from Chang's 48 degree angle: 20 sin 48 / sin 70, about 15.8. Lee is closer.
stops.mistake: Pairing a ranger's distance with that ranger's own angle; each distance is across from the other ranger's angle.
stops.again: Two scuba divers are \(15\) m apart horizontally. A turtle below them is at angles of depression \(55^\circ\) from Ana and \(48^\circ\) from Ben. How far is each diver from the turtle?
stops.againA: Third angle \(77^\circ\). Ana: \(\tfrac{15\sin 48^\circ}{\sin 77^\circ}\approx 11.4\) m. Ben: \(\tfrac{15\sin 55^\circ}{\sin 77^\circ}\approx 12.6\) m.
stops.reflect: Why is the ranger with the bigger angle always the closer one?

stops.title: Turn angles: Law of Cosines
stops.target: A turn or heading change is measured from straight ahead. Convert it to the angle inside the triangle (\(180^\circ\) minus the turn), then use the Law of Cosines.
stops.cold: A hiker walks \(6\) miles, turns \(40^\circ\) to the left, and walks \(4\) more miles. How far is the hiker from the start, in a straight line?[[graph:T5q]]
stops.coldPlain: A hiker walks 6 miles, turns 40 degrees to the left, and walks 4 more miles. How far is the hiker from the start, in a straight line?
stops.note: Show your labeled sketch: which side is opposite, adjacent, or the hypotenuse (or which law applies), and say why. Check that the answer makes sense in the situation.
stops.graphNote: There's a labeled sketch on the page. I'll describe what I drew.
stops.solution: The 40 degree turn is measured from straight ahead, so the angle inside the triangle is 140 degrees. SAS: d^2 = 36 + 16 - 48 cos 140, about 88.77, so d is about 9.4 miles.
stops.mistake: Putting 40 degrees into the Law of Cosines; that gives about 3.9 miles, too short for a hiker who barely turned.
stops.again: Two planes leave an airport, one on a heading of \(50^\circ\) and the other on \(130^\circ\). One is \(30\) mi out and the other \(45\) mi out. How far apart are they?
stops.reflect: How can a quick sketch stop you from using the turn angle by mistake?

stops.title: Three known lengths: Law of Cosines for an angle
stops.target: With three sides (SSS), use \(\cos C = \dfrac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab}\), where \(c\) is the side across from the angle you want. Keep full decimals until the end.
stops.cold: A bridge brace is a triangle with sides \(60\), \(75\), and \(90\) ft. Find the largest angle of the brace.[[graph:T6q]]
stops.coldPlain: A bridge brace is a triangle with sides 60, 75, and 90 ft. Find the largest angle.
stops.note: Show your labeled sketch: which side is opposite, adjacent, or the hypotenuse (or which law applies), and say why. Check that the answer makes sense in the situation.
stops.graphNote: There's a labeled sketch on the page. I'll describe what I drew.
stops.solution: The largest angle is across from 90. cos C = (3600 + 5625 - 8100)/9000 = 0.125, C about 82.8 degrees.
stops.mistake: Subtracting the wrong side: the side across from the angle you want is the one subtracted.
stops.again: A carpenter joins boards of \(12\) in and \(16\) in. The free ends are \(20.3\) in apart. What angle do the boards make? Is it a right angle?
stops.againA: \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{144 + 256 - 20.3^2}{2(12)(16)}\approx -0.0315\), \(\theta\approx 91.8^\circ\). Not quite square (a right angle would need exactly 20 in).
stops.reflect: Why should you keep full decimals in the calculator until the last step?

stops.title: Periodic models: the Ferris wheel
stops.target: Build a sinusoid from a story: midline and amplitude from the max and min, B from the period, and sine or cosine from where it starts.
stops.cold: A Ferris wheel is \(50\) m in diameter, and its lowest point is \(2\) m above the ground. One turn takes \(8\) minutes, and a rider boards at the bottom. Write \(h(t)\), the rider's height after \(t\) minutes, and find \(h(1)\).
stops.coldPlain: A Ferris wheel is 50 m in diameter, lowest point 2 m above the ground, one turn takes 8 minutes, and a rider boards at the bottom. Write h(t) and find h(1).
stops.note: Show the midline, amplitude, period, and why you chose sine or cosine.
stops.solution: Max 52, min 2, so the midline is 27 and the amplitude is 25. Period 8 gives B = 2 pi/8 = pi/4. Starting at the bottom (a minimum) means -cos: h(t) = 27 - 25 cos(pi t/4). h(1) = 27 - 25 cos(pi/4), about 9.3 m.
stops.mistake: Using +cos, which starts the rider at the top (52 m) instead of the bottom.
stops.again: Wheel diameter \(40\) m, lowest point \(3\) m, one turn every \(6\) minutes, board at the bottom. Write \(h(t)\) and find \(h(1)\).
stops.reflect: How would the model change if the rider started at the midline going up?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same format as the TE6 CheckIt: one right-triangle situation and one non-right triangle situation.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Solve trigonometry applications: sketch, choose right-triangle trig, the Law of Sines, or the Law of Cosines, and answer the question asked with units.
stops.cold:
(1) Nina stands on top of a cliff \(450\) ft above a lake. She sees a boat and measures an angle of depression of \(14^\circ\). How far away from Nina is the boat? (Nearest foot.)
(2) A lost boat sees two lighthouses and measures an angle of \(35^\circ\) between them. The person in the red lighthouse reports that the lighthouses are \(24\) miles apart and sees an angle of \(70^\circ\) between the boat and the other lighthouse. How far is the boat from each lighthouse? (Nearest tenth.)
stops.coldPlain: (1) Nina is on a cliff 450 ft above a lake; angle of depression to a boat 14 degrees. How far is the boat from Nina? (2) A boat measures 35 degrees between two lighthouses that are 24 miles apart; the red lighthouse sees 70 degrees between the boat and the other lighthouse. How far is the boat from each lighthouse?
stops.note: Show your labeled sketch: which side is opposite, adjacent, or the hypotenuse (or which law applies), and say why. Check that the answer makes sense in the situation.
stops.coldA: (1) About \(1{,}860\) ft: \(\tfrac{450}{\sin 14^\circ}\).[[graph:F1s]](2) About \(40.4\) mi from the red lighthouse and \(39.3\) mi from the other.[[graph:SF2]][[graph:F2s]]
stops.solution: (1) The depression angle equals the elevation angle at the boat; 450 is opposite and the distance is the hypotenuse: 450/sin 14, about 1,860 ft. (2) Third angle 75 degrees at the other lighthouse. Boat to other lighthouse is across from 70: 24 sin 70/sin 35, about 39.3 mi. Boat to red lighthouse is across from 75: 24 sin 75/sin 35, about 40.4 mi.
stops.mistake: In (2), giving the distance to the red lighthouse using the 70 degree angle measured at the red lighthouse itself.
stops.again: (1) A plane climbs at \(12^\circ\). How far along the ground does it travel to reach \(8000\) ft? (2) A bridge brace has sides \(55\), \(70\), and \(85\) ft. Find its smallest angle.
stops.againA: (1) \(\tfrac{8000}{\tan 12^\circ}\approx 37{,}637\) ft \(\approx 7.1\) mi. (2) Smallest angle is across from 55: \(\cos\theta = \tfrac{70^2 + 85^2 - 55^2}{2(70)(85)}\), \(\theta\approx 40.1^\circ\).
stops.reflect: Which step is hardest for you: drawing the picture, choosing the tool, or the calculation?
